When Sir Edward Stubbs arrived at Singapore on his way Home to receive his new appointment as Governor of Jamaica he was approached by the representative of a Straits paper for an interview regarding conditions in China. Sir Edward replied that the request was a very difficult one to comply with, as he had been on the high seas for five days and was out of touch with events in the troubled republic. This was no polite attempt to evade being interviewed — Sir Edward was courtesy itself in answering the reporter's questions—but was simply a statement of cold fact. Five days can see the most startling changes in the Chinese political situation—the enemies of yesterday the friends of to-day, and the friends of to-day the potential enemies of to-morrow. One week Wu Pei-fu is a spent force, the next he is heading a powerful new alliance. From almost absolute power Chang Tso-lin toples to the brink of ruin—a turn of the wheel and he is as strong as ever again. Thus it is with every leading figure in China today. Nobody can predict what the morrow will bring. Five weeks or five days may see the stage swept clean and a new set of actors strutting before the limelight. But if this has been the rule for the actors in the grim farce, the setting so far has been left undisturbed. The Powers have held aloof, and so far have not been forced to intervene. Russia is the only one who has taken a hand in the game to any extent, and her action has been confined to underground intriguing. But now there is a change, and ironically enough Russia is the nation concerned. For the moment it seems that the Chinese are not to be left to play out the game by themselves. The stage is no longer left free for the warlords to spin out their own little strifes. They have called down the wrath of Russia, and they have brought an outsider into the game.
But like so many of the turns of the wheel, this one it seems will have no abiding results. Russia is playing her own little game, and

If you are an ingenuity man, now far she feels can force the issue is rather a matter for interest than for anxiety. Russia is prepared to play with fire in China as anywhere else, but she is not ready to brook the international consequences that would follow the passing of a certain point. Although this latest turn of the wheel is like to have no direct outcome, it may, as a further touch of irony, have at least one good result. The other Powers have nothing in common with Russia, but they cannot fail to benefit from the sharp lesson which Russia's action must prove to the warlords who are only too apt to forget that the Powers cannot be bearded with impunity for ever. Thus, without entering into the merits of the present dispute, it can be said that Russia's action is doubly ironical in a land were amazing political events happen almost every

It is a privilege to pay tribute to one of the best utterances—among many in a single evening—by a public man, ever made in Hongkong. On the eve of Mr. Holyoak's entrance to the life of the Legislative Council it was said of him that he possessed that rare art—the gift of self-expression of the most lucid kind. That has been borne out on many an occasion, and was never more revealed than it was on Saturday, when the chairman and representative of the Hongkong General Chamber of Commerce, in a speech to business men in embryo dealt with one of the cardinal principles of business life—truth and the sanctity of contracts—with a directness and sincerity beyond all praise. Pilate's question: on truth remains a classicism. Mr. Holyoak accepts truth on its common interpretation and reminds us all—the individual and the nation—that it is only truth that makes a national eternal. By precept the University teaches and stands for this fact. In so far as its Commerce course is concerned we have Professor Hinton's words that the commerce taught by the department is bound up with truth and honour. Naturally, the course can not be wholly practical.—the larger issues are to be acquired in the counting house and in the marts—but on the theoretical side there must ever be the insistence on the sanctity of the contract whether it be in the nature of the spoken or written word. The Chinese merchant from time immemorial has been famous for the observance of his verbal undertaking. The early text books and travel books dealing with China have insisted on this to such an extent that the mind has become accustomed to this early picture of integrity. The picture may have become dimmed somewhat by examples to the contrary, but we shall be right in suggesting that in the main the members of the great merchant class of China have been true to their bond. Mr. Holyoak from an experience of twenty-five years, can speak convincingly of what he knows and can say how well the nations of China and Britain have carried truth and honour into effect. The abandonment of these great principles brings corruption and destruction. There is no need here to cite examples in support of this elementary contention. The Commerce Course at the University is based on sound principles and has nothing to do with what is popularly known as "legalised piracy." It is to the credit of the University that it has initiated and maintained the course and that it
is out to emphasise the sanctity of those things, without which it would be impossible to carry on and maintain at least full vigour the trade and commerce of nations.

In a leading article on the new Emergency Ordinance in the Strains Settlements, the "Strains Times" gives strong support to the measures to be adopted in cases of emergency or public danger, pointing to the experiences of Hongkong as a most useful precedent. It reminds its readers that there are tens of thousands of Chinese in the Strains who are members of secret societies, and that thousands of these possess such deadly weapons as automatic pistols. "Common sense tells us," says our contemporary, "that we ought to be prepared, because the south of China is swarming with emissaries of Bolsheviks, which cherishes a furious, hatred of all things British, and has already found the ignorant classes of Chinese ready tools for its purpose." It recalls that in a petition recently presented to the Strains Governor by the master tailors of Singapore there were given the names of men sent there from Canton to foment labour trouble, and no one should be under any delusion that they proceeded there as friends of labour. They went simply as enemies of British institutions, and labour is merely the tool they are using. Moreover, nine-tenths of those who are serving the Bolsheviks emissaries are Chinese aliens in the Strains and the "Strains Times" asks: "Have aliens any right to enter our territory and dictate the terms on which they will work? Have Bolsheviks agents any right to order employers living under British law to obey some Moscow or Canton commands? We decidedly say no, and we want a law strong enough to snuff out the impertinence as soon as it appears." It is evident that the lessons gained from the experiences of Hongkong have not been lost so far as our sister Colony is concerned, and that in itself is all to the good.

Reports from Paris state that whilst passing through Paris on his return journey from Rappallo to London Sir Austen Chamberlain will confer with the French Premier, M. Briand. It is assumed that the conversations will cover various outstanding questions such as the German disarmament measures and the German request for a reduction of the occupation army.

The French newspapers are discussing the likelihood of a postponement of the preparatory conference on general disarmament; which is scheduled to meet at Geneva under the auspices of the League of Nations on February 15.

Although no wish for postponement has been expressed by the British Government, which is in readiness to proceed with the work of the conference, it would doubtless agree, if such a course appeared desirable.
The "Cabinet has decided to accept the League of Nations' invitation to Germany to participate in the preliminary Disarmament Conference.
"Le Matin" understands that the main item in the next conversations between M. Briand and Sir "Austen Chamberlain" will probably be the postponement of the preliminary disarmament conference.
Meanwhile, the French Government is endeavouring to bring about a diplomatic rapprochement between Russia and Switzerland.

“The Red Flag” is not good enough.....If I were a middle-class Tory, I should be perfectly certain that the Labour Party would never conquer so long as it marches to that sort of music.—Ramsay MacDonald.

"The Red Flag" stirs the blood. It wakens the spool. It fills the spirit. It may not be classical music. It may not be high-class poetry; but it fills the bill.—Ben Turner (chairman of the "Daily Herald" Directors).
...this wretched ditty. "The Red Flag," with its cheap rhetoric and doleful tune," is utterly banal throughout. Long since dead sentiment must not be allowed to defer the interment.—Norman D. Shaith.

If some of our leaders are getting too respectable to have any use for "The Red Flag," the Labour women of Merthyr are still going to remain loyal to it.—Resolution passed by the Merthyr I.L.P. Women's Group.
I think "The Red Flag" will live for a bit yet.—Jim Connell (who wrote the words).

Jazz is going to be the music of the future. I will go further, and say that jazz is going to be the opera of the future. If any composer can come to me with a well-developed jazz opera I will produce it at the Metropolitan Opera House as a national duty.—Otto Kahn
I like "jazz," not as pure music, but as a curiosity.—Serge Kussewitzky.
Everybody who loves dancing and dance music will agree with Mr. Billy Merson's attack on "jazz." But "jazz" has been dead for at least four years.—Con-

Mr. Stanley Baldwin, Prime Minister, in a speech at the Unionist Association dinner in London, said that unless great economies were secured an increase taxation this year or next, whatever Government was in power, will be inevitable.
The Premier thankfully noted the hopeful signs of trade improvement. He declared that economies must be made involving the sacrifices not only of luxuries but of things almost in the category of necessities. He stated that the eyes of their opponents were fixed more on spending rather than saving, and the Government would need the stoutest support of all its friends in forgoing the same.
He claimed a record year for legislation; enumerating the satisfactory measures for settling foreign and democratic difficulties, in which social reform had a prominent place.
President Coolidge has modined the court-martial sentence "on Colonel Mitchell and ruled that he should receive full army allowance and half pay, amounting to $397 per month during his suspension.

[The Court Martial-upheld, all eight counts charged against Mitchell, finding him guilty of conduct, prejudicial to the good order of military discipline, insubordination, and utterances contemptuous to the United States War and Navy Departments. He was suspended for five years.]

"Jazz" is not deeply rooted in the affections of the people. It is like an over-spiced sauce, added to an old bone. I can listen to it for ten minutes, but after that I am in despair. I think the day of "Jazz" is over.—Bruno Walter.

John Davidson, a true poet and fine critic, lived through many years of financial hardship, only to die by his own hand in despair at his failure. Davidson often acted as a reader for John. One day he wrote to the publisher that he had just finished reading a novel of rare passion and power—the naked and unashamed work, probably, of a woman mature with erotic experience. Lane wrote to the author—one Miss Vivian Corry—stated that he wanted to publish the book, but that there were certain rather questionable passages in the work which required discussion. "Imagine my surprise," said Lane in telling the story, "when a girl of about 17 was ushered in. My dear young lady, I said, 'It's the author of this book that I wanted to see; I can't discuss such things with a child like you.' But Mr. Lane, replied this astonishing young person, 'I am the author.' And so it proved. Lane advised her to use a pen name and it was he who invented for her—from her initials—"Victoria Cross." The novel in question was called "To-morrow."
The same afternoon the sound of crashing furniture brought the Queen hurrying into the room to find the Princess scarlet with rage and a bruised governess moaning in the corner.
There was once a certain Princess who
could not keep her temper. She was exhorted by the Queen, to say the Lord's Prayer through slowly whenever she felt a fit of rage coming on.

"You didn't do what I ordered," said the Queen sternly.
"I did, Ma," said the Princess, "if I hadn't I should have broken her blooming neck."
The Senate, has, by 68 votes to 26, adopted a motion applying the closure, thus ensuring a final vote in the debate on adherence to the World Court within a few days.

Washington, later.
To-day's debate was led by Senator Robinson, who, retorting to interruptions, said that the whole Ku Klux Klam was opposed to American membership of the World Court. Senator Robinson in this connection mentioned Senator Reed, "but the latter promptly denied that he was in any way concerned with the Ku Klux Klam, nor had he knowledge of its relation to the question.

[Reuter cabled on Saturday: Oppents of the World Court have been holding the floor by incessant oratory. Thus, the Government is somewhat concerned as apparently the delegates must sail not later than February 6. Senator Robinson, the Democratic leader, announced that a rule limiting the debate would be invoked unless agreement for fixing the time of the roll-call was reached. The "New York Times" advises that Vice-President Dawes should cease the campaign against rules in the Senate because the Senate itself by persistently blocking public business is the best argument for the necessity of revising them. It declares that the Senate has already made itself appear "helpless, drifting, futile." The minority, taking advantage of the absolute rules, threatens to prevent not only a vote on the World Court but also the passage of the Tax Bill before the Senate.]
On a charge of misconduct in the carrying out of his duties, an Indian constable was charged at the Central Magistracy this morning and remanded for three days under medical observation.
